predictions.explanation:
The prediction has two parts: (1) that the next 6–18 months (roughly March 2022–September 2023) would feature high market volatility and uncertainty driven by unclear inflation and interest-rate paths, and (2) that over a 5–10 year horizon from 2022 the world would *not* enter a regime of persistent stagflation or sustained hyperinflation.

For the 6–18 month window, the prediction matches what happened. In 2022 global equities entered a bear market: the MSCI World Index fell about 18%, the S&P 500 dropped 19% for the year (down 25% at its October low), and the Nasdaq fell 33%, with the decline explicitly linked to the 2021–2023 inflation surge and aggressive interest-rate hikes. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_stock_market_decline?utm_source=openai))  Central banks rapidly tightened policy as inflation remained far above target, creating significant uncertainty about how high and how fast rates would rise and whether this would trigger recession. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021%E2%80%932023_inflation_surge?utm_source=openai))  The ECB’s November 2022 Financial Stability Review described markets as "fragile amid heightened macroeconomic uncertainty," noting elevated volatility in interest-rate markets as participants continually revised expectations for the monetary-policy path based on inflation data and central bank communications. ([ecb.europa.eu](https://www.ecb.europa.eu/press/financial-stability-publications/fsr/html/ecb.fsr202211~6383d08c21.en.html?utm_source=openai))  That uncertainty persisted into 2023, with the rapid rate hikes contributing to the March 2023 failure of Silicon Valley Bank and other regional banks, an episode that clearly tied market stress and volatility to the interaction of inflation and rising rates. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collapse_of_Silicon_Valley_Bank?utm_source=openai))  So the short- to medium-term part of his forecast was essentially correct.

For the 5–10 year horizon claim (no persistent global stagflation or new hyperinflation regime), not enough time has elapsed to give a firm verdict. Evidence so far is *consistent* with his view: in major advanced economies, inflation peaked in 2022 and then fell back toward the low single digits by 2023–2024 (e.g., U.S. CPI eased from around 8% in 2022 to roughly 3–4% in 2023–2024), while growth remained positive and unemployment relatively low, which is the opposite of entrenched stagflation. ([usinflationcalculator.com](https://www.usinflationcalculator.com/inflation/current-inflation-rates/?utm_source=openai))  The IMF’s recent outlook projects global inflation continuing to decline toward mid-single-digit rates rather than accelerating into any hyperinflationary spiral. ([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/markets/us/imf-lifts-us-outlook-warns-countries-against-protectionism-subsidies-2025-01-17/?utm_source=openai))  However, his statement explicitly covers 5–10 years from 2022 (through roughly 2027–2032). As of late 2025 we are only about 3½ years into that window, so it is too early to say definitively that the world *will not* experience persistent stagflation or a structurally new hyperinflationary regime over the full horizon.

Because the near-term volatility/uncertainty call has clearly been borne out but the longer-horizon global stagflation/hyperinflation claim cannot yet be fully tested, the overall prediction must be rated as **inconclusive (too early)** rather than definitively right or wrong.

predictions.explanation:
Chamath said on March 26, 2022 that **“the markets are mostly moving upwards for the short term”** and then **“volatility is going to come back.”**

Looking at broad U.S. equity indices after that date:

- The S&P 500 weekly closes show **4,543 on March 25, 2022** (the day before the podcast release) and then **4,545 on April 1**, followed by a steady slide to **4,488 (Apr 8), 4,393 (Apr 15), 4,272 (Apr 22), and 4,132 (Apr 29)**, continuing downward into May and June.
  This is a **clear downtrend starting almost immediately after late March**, not a period where markets were “mostly moving upwards.” ([fedprimerate.com](https://www.fedprimerate.com/s-and-p-500-history.htm?utm_source=openai))
- On a monthly basis, the S&P 500 returned **+3.83% in March 2022**, but then **-8.99% in April, roughly flat in May (+0.04%), and -8.78% in June**. ([statmuse.com](https://www.statmuse.com/money/ask/s-and-p-500-monthly-returns-from-2022?utm_source=openai))  Over the “next few weeks to a few months” after late March, the index was predominantly down or flat.
- The tech‑heavy Nasdaq did even worse, with **monthly returns of +3.67% in March but then -13.56% in April, -2.03% in May, and -9.43% in June 2022**, reflecting a sharp and sustained selloff rather than a short‑term upward trend. ([statmuse.com](https://www.statmuse.com/money/ask/nasdaq-chart-by-month-2022?utm_source=openai))
- A Business Insider summary of the March 2022 “death cross” notes that after that signal in March 2022, the **S&P 500 went on to fall about 16% and the Nasdaq about 27%**, underscoring that the subsequent move was decisively downward. ([businessinsider.com](https://www.businessinsider.com/death-cross-pattern-spx-ndx-stock-market-outlook-bearish-signal-2025-4?utm_source=openai))

On volatility, the **Cboe VIX Index** remained elevated as the market slid into a >20% drawdown by June 30, 2022, when the S&P 500 was down about **20.5% over six months** and the VIX closed at **28.71**, well above its long‑run average. ([cboe.com](https://www.cboe.com/insights/posts/the-vix-index-and-muted-volatility-in-2022/?utm_source=openai))  But this was *continuation* of high volatility rather than a calm “upward” period followed by volatility “coming back.”

Because the core, time‑bounded part of his prediction—that **broad equity markets would mostly trend upward in the immediate short term (weeks to a few months) starting from late March 2022**—was not borne out (they mostly went down and entered a bear market instead), the prediction is best classified as **wrong**, even though volatility indeed remained or became elevated.

predictions.explanation:
Evidence from 2022–2023 shows that late‑stage private SaaS/software companies experienced exactly the valuation compression and financing difficulty Chamath anticipated.

* **Sharp valuation markdowns in SaaS:** TechCrunch reported that SaaS valuations fell ~75% from October 2021 to October 2022, creating a “perfect storm for companies needing follow‑on funding,” as exits collapsed and investors reassessed richly valued SaaS names. ([techcrunch.com](https://techcrunch.com/2023/10/26/saas-follow-on-rounds-slowdown/?utm_source=openai)) An analysis of SaaS valuations similarly notes that companies which previously raised at 100x ARR might have to refinance near 20x ARR, with late‑stage investors “shunning the late-stage private financing market” because prior rounds were too expensive. ([paddle.com](https://www.paddle.com/blog/saas-valuations-are-changing?utm_source=openai))

* **Late‑stage software/SaaS specifically flagged as most at risk:** In April 2022, TechCrunch highlighted that *late‑stage software/SaaS startups* were “in the most valuation trouble,” as their revenue multiples had been bid up the most in 2020–2021 and were now retracing in line with public software stocks. ([techcrunch.com](https://techcrunch.com/2022/04/01/late-stage-software-startups-might-be-in-the-most-valuation-trouble/?utm_source=openai)) This directly matches Chamath’s concern that the repricing of public SaaS would spill over into late‑stage private SaaS.

* **Severe late‑stage valuation resets in 2022:** Carta’s 2022 data show that by Q4 2022, median valuations for late‑stage rounds had collapsed: Series D valuations were down 58% year‑over‑year and Series E+ down 72%. The median Series D round size was 79% smaller than a year earlier, and Carta describes late‑stage fundraising as “difficult,” with far fewer, much smaller deals at much lower valuations. ([carta.com](https://carta.com/data/state-of-private-markets-q4-2022/?utm_source=openai))

* **Ongoing late‑stage funding trouble in 2023:** Carta’s Q1 2023 update shows median Series D valuations down ~70% year‑over‑year and Series E+ down 82%, calling it “a difficult start to 2023 for late-stage startups hunting for new venture capital.” ([carta.com](https://carta.com/data/late-stage-vc-valuations-q1-2023/?utm_source=openai)) TechCrunch likewise described the “late‑stage venture market” as “crumbling,” noting median valuations for Series D+ rounds had fallen about 60% and that late‑stage deal counts were plunging. ([techcrunch.com](https://techcrunch.com/2023/08/23/late-stage-evaporating/?utm_source=openai))

* **Financing environment clearly worse for late‑stage SaaS:** A TechCrunch piece focused on SaaS follow‑on rounds observed that venture investment fell 70% in Q4 2022 vs. Q4 2021 and that overvalued SaaS names, combined with a collapse in exits, were particularly hurting companies trying to raise extension and follow‑on rounds. ([techcrunch.com](https://techcrunch.com/2023/10/26/saas-follow-on-rounds-slowdown/?utm_source=openai)) That is precisely the “trouble” Chamath was pointing to: not just paper markdowns, but real difficulty raising capital at prior valuations.

Across multiple independent datasets (Carta, Crunchbase, SVB) and SaaS‑specific analyses, late‑stage private SaaS/software companies saw large valuation markdowns, a spike in down/flat rounds, and a significant pullback in late‑stage capital in 2022–2023. This matches the substance and timing of Chamath’s prediction, so it is best scored as **right**.

Over 80% of unicorns (many SaaS) saw lower valuations ([Industry Ventures](https://www.industryventures.com/insight/thinning-the-herd/)). Financing involved more bridge/extension rounds at lower terms, confirming troubles during the specified period.

predictions.explanation:
The core claim was that among the big late‑stage, VC‑backed companies waiting to go public in early 2022, **some would ultimately IPO at valuations below their last private round (down‑round IPOs) during the next IPO cycle (2022–2023).**

That happened clearly:

- **Instacart (Maplebear)** was one of the marquee late‑stage unicorns in the 2021–2022 IPO backlog; CNBC in March 2021 noted its valuation had just doubled to **$39B** and that it was preparing for a “highly anticipated public debut,” with Goldman Sachs expected to lead the IPO. ([cnbc.com](https://www.cnbc.com/2021/03/02/instacarts-valuation-doubles-to-39-billion.html?utm_source=openai)) When Instacart finally went public in September 2023, its IPO priced at $30 per share, implying a **fully diluted valuation of about $9.9B**, a steep drop from the $39B private round two years earlier. ([fortune.com](https://fortune.com/2023/09/18/instacart-ipo-value/?utm_source=openai)) Axios explicitly labeled this a **“down‑round IPO,”** noting Instacart raised $660M at a $9.9B valuation, sharply below the $39B valuation of its March 2021 funding round. ([axios.com](https://www.axios.com/2023/09/19/instacarts-ipo-venture-capital?utm_source=openai)) This single, very prominent example already satisfies “some of them are probably going to have to IPO at down rounds.”

- The broader pattern shows a **meaningful subset**, not just one outlier. For example, Arm’s 2023 IPO valued it at **$54.5B**, below an internal $64B valuation SoftBank had assigned shortly before, which market commentary described as a down‑round IPO alongside Instacart’s sharply reduced range of **$8.6–$9.3B** vs. its prior $39B private valuation. ([nasdaq.com](https://www.nasdaq.com/articles/latam-tech-weekly-arms-debut-and-more-to-follow?utm_source=openai)) Klaviyo, another late‑stage startup in that cohort, went public in September 2023 at about **$9.2B**, roughly in line with or slightly below its prior late‑stage valuation around $9.5B, and was reported as initially targeting an IPO valuation *below* its last private round. ([cnbc.com](https://www.cnbc.com/2023/09/19/klaviyo-considers-pricing-ipo-at-top-of-range-or-above-reuters.html?utm_source=openai))

- More generally, venture commentators summarized the 2023–2024 IPO window as being dominated by down‑round IPOs: a widely cited analysis by investor Aman Verjee (shared by Dave McClure) noted that **“just about every VC‑backed IPO in 2023 and 2024 was a ‘down round’”** relative to the prior private financing, explicitly listing **Instacart, Reddit, Klaviyo, ServiceTitan, Circle, and Hinge Health** as examples. ([linkedin.com](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/davemcclure_every-vc-backed-ipo-in-the-past-12-months-activity-7334245985251983361-m1vv?utm_source=openai)) This confirms that down‑round IPOs became common among the very cohort of late‑stage, VC‑backed companies Sacks was talking about.

Because at least one flagship backlog name (Instacart) and then a broader set of peer companies *did* IPO at valuations below their last private rounds within the ensuing IPO cycle (by late 2023), Sacks’s prediction that “some of them are probably going to have to IPO at down rounds” is borne out by subsequent events.

predictions.explanation:
The prediction requires knowing what share of all companies that IPOed between roughly 26 March 2022 and 25 March 2023 did so at valuations below their last private financing round.

The best available aggregate data on “down‑round IPOs” comes from proprietary datasets used by Silicon Valley Bank (SVB), PitchBook, and others. SVB’s 2025 *State of the Markets* and related summaries state that historically down‑round IPOs have made up about 30–50% of VC‑backed tech IPOs, and that in 2024 specifically, 4 of 7 US VC‑backed tech IPOs (≈57%) were down rounds, but they do **not** publish a clear, year‑by‑year figure for 2022 or for the exact March‑to‑March window you care about ([scribd.com](https://www.scribd.com/document/883716658/State-of-the-Markets-h1-2025?utm_source=openai)). Other reporting and analyses (e.g., The Information and investor commentary) document that by 2023–24, “just about every” VC‑backed IPO or the last several VC‑backed IPOs in a 12‑month span were down rounds, but again these claims cover later periods (2023–25) and not specifically March 2022–March 2023 ([linkedin.com](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/davemcclure_every-vc-backed-ipo-in-the-past-12-months-activity-7334245985251983361-m1vv?utm_source=openai)).

Moreover, public datasets on global or US IPOs in 2022–early 2023 generally track IPO counts and proceeds, not whether each deal’s IPO valuation was above or below its last private round; many offerings in that period are carve‑outs or non‑VC‑backed firms where a “last private financing round” isn’t well defined ([scribd.com](https://www.scribd.com/document/704183915/SVB-s-Innovation-Economy-H2-2023-Outlook?utm_source=openai)). Without a comprehensive, auditable list of all IPOs in that specific 12‑month window matched to their last private valuations, it isn’t possible to credibly determine whether **more than 50%** were down‑round IPOs.

Because the necessary granular data for that exact period and population is not publicly available, the correctness of the prediction cannot be determined with confidence. Therefore the outcome is **ambiguous** rather than clearly right or wrong.

predictions.explanation:
Chamath’s claim had two parts: (1) late‑stage private tech names like Gopuff, Canva, Klarna, Discord, Ripple, Grammarly “have to” be marked down ~15–40% immediately as rates rise, and (2) if they keep growing strongly, they can *recover to prior peak valuations within about 18 months* of that markdown.

What actually happened with the concrete examples he cited:

- **Klarna** – Peak valuation was about $45.6B in June 2021. By July 2022 it raised at $6.7B, an ~85% markdown, far beyond the 15–40% range. Even by 2025 its IPO valuation talk/targets are only around $12.5–15B, still far below the $45.6B peak, years after the markdown. ([cnbc.com](https://www.cnbc.com/2022/07/11/klarna-valuation-plunges-85percent-as-buy-now-pay-later-hype-fades.html?utm_source=openai))
- **Gopuff** – Valued around $15B in 2021. Subsequent financing in 2025 values it at about $8.5B, a drop of roughly 40–45%, and it has *not* returned to the prior peak more than three years later. ([ft.com](https://www.ft.com/content/6941ce62-91ce-4e84-a3c0-3734635f27a3?utm_source=openai))
- **Canva** – Valued at $40B in 2021. Blackbird Ventures marked its position down ~36% to $25.6B in mid‑2022, and T. Rowe Price later marked its stake down roughly 67.6%, again deeper than Chamath’s 15–40% band. Canva only re‑attained and then exceeded the prior peak via secondary/staff share sales at around $42B in 2025—roughly three to four years after the 2021 peak and about three years after the first markdown, not within 18 months. ([startupdaily.net](https://www.startupdaily.net/topic/business/exit-stage-bright-blackbird-offloads-150-million-slice-of-its-canva-stake-at-39-billion-valuation/?utm_source=openai))
- **Discord** – Raised at a $15B valuation in 2021. By mid‑2023, Fidelity had marked its holdings in Discord down about 47% from cost, with no public evidence that valuations had returned to the 2021 peak within 18 months of the markdown. ([techcrunch.com](https://techcrunch.com/2023/06/30/fidelity-deepens-valuation-cut-for-reddit-and-discord/?utm_source=openai))
- **Grammarly** – Was valued at $13B in 2021; later coverage still references that 2021 figure, and recent financings are structured as non‑dilutive debt rather than new equity rounds, suggesting no clear equity repricing back to a meaningfully higher valuation. There is also no public indication of a clean 15–40% markdown then full recovery inside 18 months. ([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/business/grammarly-secures-1-billion-general-catalyst-build-ai-productivity-platform-2025-05-29/?utm_source=openai))
- **Ripple** – Valued at about $15B in an early‑2022 buyback, then referenced around $11.3B in early 2024, implying a markdown of roughly 25%. Ripple does eventually raise at a $40B valuation in 2025, but that recovery occurs several years after the 2022 valuation event, not within an 18‑month window. ([research.contrary.com](https://research.contrary.com/company/ripple?utm_source=openai))

In the broader late‑stage market, mutual‑fund and VC markdowns in 2022–2023 were often significantly steeper than 40%, and many unicorns remained well below 2021 peak valuations through at least late 2023, despite continued revenue growth at a number of them. ([business2community.com](https://www.business2community.com/business-news-and-stories/canva-is-worth-67-6-less-than-it-was-in-2021-according-to-t-rowe-price/?utm_source=openai))

So:
- The **size** of the required markdowns was generally *larger* than his 15–40% range for the emblematic names he mentioned.
- The **timeline** for recovery was materially off: even strong performers like Canva and Ripple only got back to or above their prior peaks *years* later, while others (Klarna, Gopuff, Discord) still haven’t as of late 2025.

Because both the magnitude and the 18‑month recovery path were meaningfully wrong for the very companies cited as examples, the prediction overall is best classified as **wrong**.

predictions.explanation:
The prediction has two testable parts, and both broadly match what happened.

1. **March–Fall 2022: late‑stage private VC effectively “shut” at prior peak valuations**  
   * Global venture funding in 2022 fell 35% from the 2021 record, with the sharpest damage in large late‑stage/mega‑rounds (funding for $100M+ rounds dropped 49%), indicating that the late‑stage growth market bore the brunt of the pullback.
   ([cbinsights.com](https://www.cbinsights.com/research/report/venture-trends-2022/?utm_source=openai))  
   * PitchBook data showed late‑stage deal value in Q3 2022 at an 11‑quarter low, with the median late‑stage valuation down ~29% from Q1 2022 and the “top of the market all but disappearing,” as crossover investors (Tiger, SoftBank, etc.) largely stepped back from new high‑valuation late‑stage deals.
   ([siliconangle.com](https://siliconangle.com/2022/11/08/pitchbook-late-stage-venture-capital-valuations-fall-2021-highs/?utm_source=openai))  
   * A 2024 interview with a major secondaries platform (Forge/Proskauer) described private markets between roughly June 2022 and June 2023 as “for all intents and purposes, shut” because buyers could not agree on fair value; there were many more sellers than buyers and bid–ask spreads were wide, a textbook buyer–seller standoff.
   ([jdsupra.com](https://www.jdsupra.com/legalnews/podcast-private-market-talks-designing-8365005/?utm_source=openai))  
   * Country‑level data (e.g., India) show late‑stage funding in 2022 down ~48% while early‑stage was roughly flat, underscoring that it was late‑stage/growth rounds, not seed, that froze first.
   ([theweek.in](https://www.theweek.in/theweek/business/2023/01/28/startup-industry-issues-fund-crunch.amp.html?utm_source=openai))  
   Together, these data support the claim that from spring through at least fall 2022, new late‑stage primary financings at 2021‑style peak valuations were extremely rare and the market was, in practical terms, “closed” at those levels due to a valuation impasse between buyers and sellers.

2. **No return to 2020–21 late‑stage valuation extremes in the subsequent cycle (through 2025)**  
   * CB Insights reports that by 2023 the *median late‑stage deal size* had fallen more than 50% from 2021 ($21M vs. $50M), reflecting both fewer mega‑rounds and a structurally lower pricing environment rather than a snap‑back to 2021 conditions.
   ([cbinsights.com](https://www.cbinsights.com/research/report/venture-trends-2023/?utm_source=openai))  
   * Carta’s 2024 late‑stage analysis shows Series D median valuations at about $212M in Q1 2024 versus a peak of $1.07B in Q3 2021, and Series E+ medians at ~$841M vs. nearly $1.6B in Q2 2022—still dramatically below prior highs despite some rebound.
   ([carta.com](https://carta.com/uk/en/data/late-stage-lull-2024/?utm_source=openai))  
   * Angel Capital Association data similarly show growth‑stage valuations resetting: Series B medians fell from $32M (2021 peak) to $19M in 2024, and Series C+ from $75M (2022 high) to $35M in 2024.
   ([angelcapitalassociation.org](https://angelcapitalassociation.org/blog/the-early-stage-valuation-disconnect/?utm_source=openai))  
   * Market‑wide volumes and valuations have not re‑approached 2021 levels: global 2024 VC funding was still about 55% below the 2021 peak, even after an AI‑driven uptick, and exit value remains far beneath 2021 as well.
   ([barrons.com](https://www.barrons.com/articles/venture-capital-investments-2024-ai-766c99dc?utm_source=openai))  
   * Regional data echo this structural reset. For example, late‑stage PE‑VC funding into Indian companies fell from $23.4B in 2021 to about $9B in 2024, with local investors explicitly describing 2021 as an anomaly driven by excess liquidity and stating that the “low‑cost, high‑growth days of the past may not return.”
   ([timesofindia.indiatimes.com](https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/business/india-business/pe-vc-funding-in-late-stage-cos-dips-as-investors-turn-cautious/articleshow/120109627.cms?utm_source=openai))  

   There *are* pockets of froth—most notably large generative‑AI rounds in 2024–25, where some startups have reached extreme valuations and even prompted bubble warnings.
   ([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/legal/transactional/ai-startup-valuations-raise-bubble-fears-funding-surges-2025-10-03/?utm_source=openai))  But those are concentrated in a narrow sector; broad late‑stage medians and deal sizes remain far below 2021–early‑2022 levels.

Given that (a) late‑stage funding at peak valuations largely stalled from mid‑2022 onward due to a valuation disconnect, and (b) market‑wide late‑stage valuations and deal sizes have not returned to the extreme multiples of the preceding 18 months through at least late 2025, the prediction is best categorized as **right** overall, allowing for rhetorical overstatement and a few sector‑specific exceptions.

predictions.explanation:
Brad Gerstner said in March 2022 that real price discovery for late‑stage private tech companies would *start in fall 2022* once companies needed money or chose to go public. ([podscripts.co](https://podscripts.co/podcasts/all-in-with-chamath-jason-sacks-friedberg/e73-late-stage-vc-markdowns-and-mistakes-market-strategy-ukrainerussia-update-with-brad-gerstner?utm_source=openai))

What actually happened was an extended freeze. The IPO window effectively closed in 2022: by late October there had been only 167 US IPOs, about 80% fewer than by the same date in 2021, and venture-backed tech IPOs largely stopped, so there were very few public listings to set new, market‑clearing prices for unicorns. ([fabricaventures.com](https://fabricaventures.com/zero-ipo/?utm_source=openai)) At the same time, many late‑stage startups had raised unusually large rounds in 2020–21. A 2022 investor letter noted that around two‑thirds of unicorns still had more than 18 months of runway in 2H 2022, and that IPO windows remained shut; secondary trades had moved to roughly a 50% discount to the last round, but secondary volume was still ‘tempered’ and bid–ask spreads were only beginning to narrow. ([medium.com](https://medium.com/%40verdure/2022-annual-letter-83909a8e5e57?utm_source=openai)) That is not a setting where lots of companies are forced into transparent, price‑revealing primary financings or IPOs.

Private financing data and contemporaneous commentary show that broad repricing was delayed into 2023–24 rather than starting in fall 2022. PitchBook’s 2023 US VC Valuations report finds that down rounds were just 14.2% of financings in 2023 (the highest since 2017, but still a minority) and emphasizes that many late‑stage companies were stretching time between rounds—often 24–30 months after 2021 highs—and relying on structured terms instead of clean repricings, with more forced raises and down rounds expected going forward. ([scribd.com](https://www.scribd.com/document/708534139/2023-Annual-US-VC-Valuations-Report?utm_source=openai)) Early 2023 remarks from Chamath Palihapitiya likewise describe late‑stage boards refusing to budge on valuation and using convertibles specifically to avoid ‘true price discovery’ in the private markets. ([indigilife.com](https://indigilife.com/chamath-palihapitiya-it-could-take-three-years-for-the-market-to-accurately-reprice-late-stage-cos/?utm_source=openai)) And by November 2023, Gerstner himself was saying that because startups had raised so much in 2020–21, they hadn’t needed to fundraise on normal 9–12‑month cycles, and that *real price discovery* for late‑stage and IPO‑track companies would come in 2024, especially the back half—explicitly shifting his earlier timeline by roughly two years. ([ritholtz.com](https://ritholtz.com/2023/11/transcript-brad-gerstner/?utm_source=openai))

Because the major wave of forced late‑stage recapitalizations and IPO‑based repricings did *not* begin in fall 2022, and key participants later acknowledged that real price discovery was still mostly ahead of them, the timing component of his prediction is best judged as wrong.

predictions.explanation:
Evidence since 2022 shows exactly the kind of prolonged, complex unwinding of rate‑ and liquidity‑driven distortions that Chamath predicted.

From 2022 onward, major central banks reversed more than a decade of ultra‑low rates and QE. The Fed raised its policy rate from near zero in early 2022 to about 5.25–5.50% by July 2023 and began quantitative tightening in June 2022, shrinking its balance sheet by over $2 trillion from a ~$9T peak. A UN analysis explicitly describes this as an unwinding of QE that injected trillions in liquidity and notes that this process is proving particularly challenging.([twn.my](https://twn.my/title2/susagri/2024/sa1102.htm?utm_source=openai))

This policy shift precipitated a broad 2022 bear market: global equity indices fell sharply, with the S&P 500 down 19% and the Nasdaq down 33% for the year, driven by inflation and aggressive rate hikes. Commentators widely framed this as the popping of an “everything bubble” inflated by years of easy money.([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_stock_market_decline?utm_source=openai))

The adjustment has clearly been multi‑year rather than a brief shock. Late‑stage venture and private tech have gone through sustained markdowns and funding contraction: late‑stage VC deal volume and capital in 2023 were far below the 2021 peak and even below 2019 levels. Global venture funding in 2023 fell about 42% year‑on‑year, with growth‑stage valuations described as “down massively” from 2021; major crossover investors like Tiger Global and SoftBank slashed activity and marked down portfolios (Tiger cutting startup values by roughly a third, SoftBank reporting multi‑billion‑dollar write‑downs).([carta.com](https://carta.com/data/late-stage-2023/?utm_source=openai))

Related markets that epitomized the bubble period also went through extended unwinds. The SPAC boom of 2020–2021 collapsed in 2022–2023, with SPAC IPO counts and proceeds dropping by an order of magnitude, while IPO activity and exits overall fell to their lowest levels since the financial crisis and, even by 2024–2025, remained far below 2021 despite a partial recovery.([redbud.vc](https://redbud.vc/latest/the-crux-of-current-and-historical-vc-startup-valuation-inflations?utm_source=openai))

Real‑asset markets show a similarly drawn‑out adjustment: rapid Fed hikes doubled U.S. mortgage rates and severely distorted the housing market, while commercial property in Europe has logged multiple consecutive years of price declines linked to higher rates and financing stress, still falling in 2024.([forbes.com](https://www.forbes.com/sites/georgecalhoun/2024/03/13/collateral-damage-from-fed-policy-part-2-a-broken-housing-market/?utm_source=openai))

By late 2025, the Fed is only just preparing to stop QT after reducing its balance sheet to about $6.6–$6.7T, with analysts noting that the pandemic‑era “excess liquidity” in facilities like the reverse repo has largely been drained.([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/business/finance/fed-end-balance-sheet-reduction-december-1-2025-10-29/?utm_source=openai)) This ongoing policy normalization and the multi‑year repricing in public, private, and real‑asset markets fit Chamath’s description of “the beginning of a very complicated process of unwinding the distortion” created in the prior few years of ultra‑easy money.

Given this evidence, the prediction that 2022 would mark the start of a prolonged, complex unwinding of those distortions is best judged as **right**.

predictions.explanation:
Key elements of Brad Gerstner’s scenario did **not** occur as predicted.

1. **Missile escalation in 1–2 weeks:** Russia did continue and in some areas intensified missile and rocket attacks in early–mid April 2022 (e.g., the Kramatorsk railway station missile strike on 8 April 2022 and further strikes in Kharkiv later in April). However, such attacks were already ongoing at high intensity in March, so this was a continuation rather than a clearly identifiable, new “final straw” spike tied to negotiations. 【0search15】0search19】0search22】

2. **"Complete European embargo" of ~3 million bpd in that window:** Before the war, the EU imported around 2.2 million bpd of Russian crude and 1.2 million bpd of refined products (about 3.4 million bpd total), close to the “3 million barrels a day” figure he cited. 【1search1】1search2】1search4】1search7】  But the EU did **not** impose a complete embargo within 1–2 weeks of 26 March 2022. Instead:
   * EU leaders only agreed **in principle** to a sixth sanctions package including an oil ban at a special European Council meeting on 30–31 May 2022. 【0search4】0search6】
   * The formal sixth package, adopted on 3 June 2022, bans seaborne Russian crude and certain products, phased in over 6–8 months, and explicitly **exempts pipeline deliveries (Druzhba)** and grants other derogations. This covers about 90% of previous imports, not a 100% “complete” embargo. 【0search0【0search1【0search2【1search3】1search6】1search7】  Thus neither the **timing** (not in early April) nor the **completeness** of the embargo matches his prediction.

3. **These moves as “final straws” right before peace talks:** High‑level Russia–Ukraine negotiations (Belarus, Antalya, and especially the Istanbul talks on 29–30 March 2022) were already underway **before** the period he pointed to, and they effectively stalled in April 2022 without a settlement. 【2view0】  There was no new, major peace-negotiation phase in early/mid‑April that followed a sudden oil embargo and escalatory missile campaign as he described. Subsequent serious diplomacy did not resume until much later (2025), long after the EU’s partial oil ban. 【2view0】

Because the central, falsifiable parts of the prediction (a **complete** EU oil embargo of ~3 mbpd and its timing as the trigger “right before” negotiations) did not happen, the prediction overall is best classified as **wrong**, even though Russian missile attacks did continue and intensify in some locales around that time.
predictions.grok_explanation:
The prediction required **both** an increase in Russian missile attacks on Ukraine *and* a complete European embargo on ~3M bpd Russian oil within 1-2 weeks of March 26, 2022 (i.e., by ~April 9), as 'final straws' shortly *before* formal peace talks. 

- **No EU oil embargo**: EU discussions began ~April 2022 (e.g., non-binding resolution Apr 7, [Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/business/energy/case-against-eu-sanctions-russian-oil-2022-04-08/)), but the actual ban was announced June 2-3, 2022 (6th sanctions package, effective Dec 5 for crude, [EU Consilium](https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/policies/sanctions-against-russia/timeline-packages-sanctions-since-february-2022/), [Bruegel](https://www.bruegel.org/analysis/european-union-russia-energy-divorce-state-play)). Russian oil exports to EU continued unabated in March-April 2022 ([Dallas Fed paper](https://www.dallasfed.org/~/media/documents/research/papers/2024/wp2401r1.pdf)). 

- **Missile attacks**: Ongoing since invasion (Feb 24), with strikes like Lviv (Mar 26, [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lviv_strikes_(2022%E2%80%93present))), Kharkiv (Mar 26), but no verified *increase* or 'amp up' specifically post-Mar 26 before Apr 9; Kramatorsk strike was Apr 8 ([AP](https://apnews.com/article/russia-ukraine-invasion-war-military-0fd6866d7ee2aec12e51daa1e7c5c881)). 

- **Negotiations**: Istanbul talks began Mar 29, 2022 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peace_negotiations_in_the_Russo-Ukrainian_war_(2022%E2%80%93present))), aligning with timing, but absent escalations make full prediction fail. 

Since key elements (esp. embargo) did not occur as specified, the prediction is wrong.

predictions.explanation: Key components of Brad Gerstner’s scenario did not occur. The EU did later adopt a major embargo on Russian seaborne crude (from December 5, 2022) and most refined products (from February 5, 2023), covering about 90% of pre‑war Russian oil imports to the EU.([consilium.europa.eu](https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/policies/sanctions/restrictive-measures-against-russia-over-ukraine/sanctions-against-russia-explained/?_cldee=E0gO4YqXkuYqScrH216Q5GWUIeZNsmjub3PmZu5G1p0I3bHjNM86nmOXSbamMNx2&esid=5e60005d-ffa2-ed11-8169-005056b762b6&recipientid=contact-b6b66d37d9cfec118150005056b762b6-797c924c647e40dab5e4d8e3d3d612b8&utm_source=openai)) However, instead of collapsing, Russia’s economy experienced only a modest GDP contraction of around 2% in 2022 and then returned to growth, with estimates of roughly 3–3.6% annual GDP growth in 2023–2024, indicating strain but not economic collapse.([consilium.europa.eu](https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/infographics/impact-sanctions-russian-economy/?utm_source=openai)) On oil prices, Brent crude spiked briefly in early March 2022 to an intraday high around $139 per barrel and monthly averages peaked near $120–122, but prices never came close to the $180–$200 range he described, either at the time of the embargo’s announcement or when it took effect.([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_oil_market_chronology_from_2003?utm_source=openai)) Although there has indeed been prolonged military escalation and continued sanctions and energy measures before any decisive peace settlement, the specific quantitative claims that an EU oil embargo would both *collapse* Russia’s economy and push oil to roughly $180–$200 per barrel have clearly been falsified with several years of data, so the prediction is best judged as wrong.

predictions.grok_explanation:
The prediction required significant military/economic escalation *before* substantive post-March 2022 peace talks, specifically including a European oil embargo collapsing Russia's economy and pushing global oil to $180–200/bbl. 

- **Peace talks occurred shortly after**: Direct Russia-Ukraine talks began March 29, 2022, in Istanbul (Wikipedia; Foreign Affairs Apr 2024), with further rounds in April 2022 nearly reaching a deal. No embargo or such escalation preceded this (3 days post-podcast). Later talks (e.g., Istanbul June 2025) yielded no progress beyond prisoner swaps (Al Jazeera, BBC 2025).

- **No oil price spike**: Brent peaked ~$139/bbl on March 8, 2022 (pre-podcast); post-March 26 highs were lower (~$120-130 max in 2022), never $180-200 (EIA data; Trading Economics; Macrotrends charts).

- **EU embargo late, no collapse**: Seaborne crude ban Dec 5, 2022 (EU Council; CREA tracker). Russia's GDP fell 2.1% in 2022 but grew 3-4% in 2023-24 despite sanctions; no collapse, adapted via China/India (Chatham House Sep 2025; World Bank; Consilium infographics).

- **Military escalation yes, but specifics failed**: Ongoing fighting (ISW reports), but tied economic predictions did not materialize before or as cause for talks.

Thus, sequence and key outcomes did not occur as predicted.

predictions.explanation:
Brad argued that because China needed to protect its export‑driven economy and hit its 2022 GDP growth target of about 5.5%, it would *not* supply Russia with weapons during the Ukraine war. China did set a 2022 growth target of ~5.5% but ultimately grew only about 3%, missing that goal, so the economic premise itself did not hold as expected. ([en.people.cn](https://en.people.cn/n3/2022/0306/c90000-9966812.html?utm_source=openai))  

More importantly, open‑source trade and customs data show that Chinese state‑owned arms firms *did* supply Russia or its defense industry with weapons and critical lethal inputs after March 2022. Politico and subsequent summaries report that the state‑owned weapons manufacturer Norinco shipped assault rifles, drone parts, and body armor to Russian entities between June and December 2022, sometimes via intermediaries in Turkey and the UAE. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russo-Ukrainian_war_%282022%E2%80%93present%29?utm_source=openai))  Investigations based on customs records and New York Times reporting show that another state‑owned firm, Poly Technologies, sent large quantities of smokeless gunpowder to Russia’s Barnaul Cartridge Plant in 2022—enough propellant for at least 80 million rounds of ammunition—explicitly linking Chinese exports to Russian ammunition production. ([business-humanrights.org](https://www.business-humanrights.org/en/latest-news/china-polytech-reportedly-delivered-shipments-of-gunpowder-to-russian-munitions-factory/?utm_source=openai))  

In addition, U.S. sanctions and Reuters/AP reporting describe Chinese companies providing engines and components for Russian long‑range attack drones and other dual‑use hardware, materially enabling Russian weapons systems even when not always branded as "lethal aid." ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/49e4e56bb37ee46faf028f649df140b0?utm_source=openai))  Western analyses now characterize China as a key supplier of gunpowder, nitrocellulose, and other weapon components to Russia’s defense industry. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Support_for_Russia_in_the_Russian_invasion_of_Ukraine))  Taken together, these documented flows of assault rifles, ammunition propellant, and critical weapons components from Chinese state‑owned defense firms to Russia contradict the prediction that China would refrain from supplying Russia with weapons during the war.

predictions.grok_explanation: China has not supplied Russia with lethal weapons or finished arms systems during the Ukraine war post-March 2022, aligning with the prediction. Official Chinese statements consistently deny providing lethal weapons ([Reuters, Apr 2025](https://www.reuters.com/world/china/china-dismisses-zelenskiys-claim-it-is-supplying-weapons-russia-2025-04-18/); [USCC report](https://www.uscc.gov/research/chinas-position-russias-invasion-ukraine)). US and NATO officials confirm no direct lethal aid, despite dual-use components like machine tools, chemicals, microelectronics, and gunpowder enabling Russian production ([BBC, May 2024](https://www.bbc.com/news/60571253); [NYT, Jul 2024](https://www.nytimes.com/2024/07/10/us/politics/nato-china-russia-ukraine.html); Blinken quotes). Zelenskiy's 2025 accusations of 'weapons and gunpowder' lack independent verification and were dismissed by China as groundless; reports specify inputs to factories, not finished weapons ([Reuters, Apr/May 2025](https://www.reuters.com/world/zelenskiy-says-ukraine-has-evidence-china-supplying-russia-with-artillery-2025-04-17/)). China's 2022 GDP growth was 3% (missing 5.5% target; [official NBS, Dec 2023](https://english.www.gov.cn/news/202312/29/content_WS658ea60ac6d0868f4e8e29a1.html)), supporting prioritization of economic interests via sanction avoidance to protect exports.

predictions.explanation:
The prediction was time‑bound: by **mid‑summer 2022** the Fed would be saying it saw a *balanced* risk between growth and inflation.

In reality, the Fed’s official communications in June–July 2022 continued to **prioritize inflation risk** and explicitly described risks as *skewed*, not balanced:

- The **June 15, 2022 FOMC statement** describes elevated inflation and says, *“The Committee is highly attentive to inflation risks,”* without any language about risks being balanced between growth and inflation.
  The accompanying June minutes note that staff judged risks to real activity **skewed to the downside** and risks to inflation **skewed to the upside**, and that participants were *“highly attentive to inflation risks.”* This is the opposite of a balanced‑risks framing.

- The **July 27, 2022 FOMC statement** repeats this structure: it notes that spending and production have softened but again emphasizes that inflation is elevated and that *“The Committee is highly attentive to inflation risks”* and is *“strongly committed to returning inflation to its 2 percent objective.”* No reference is made to growth and inflation risks being in balance.

- The **July 26–27, 2022 FOMC minutes** similarly report that participants viewed the balance of risks as asymmetric: inflation risks remained **skewed to the upside**, while risks to real GDP growth were **primarily to the downside**, and they again stress that participants were highly attentive to inflation risks. This is still an explicitly one‑sided risk assessment.

- In his **July 27, 2022 press conference**, Chair Powell acknowledged two‑sided risks in a general sense but repeatedly framed policy around the need to restore price stability, calling bringing inflation down the Committee’s *“overarching focus”* and saying that failing to do so would raise the ultimate cost, stressing that this was something the Fed *“simply must do.”* That is not a claim that risks to growth and inflation were now balanced; it is an argument for prioritizing the inflation fight.

Balanced‑risk language does appear in **much later** Fed statements (e.g., in early 2024–2025, the Committee begins to say the risks to its employment and inflation goals are “moving into better balance” or “roughly in balance”), but those references are **well after** the June–July 2022 horizon of the prediction.

Because by mid‑summer 2022 the Fed was still explicitly highlighting upside inflation risk and downside growth risk, and repeatedly described itself as **highly attentive to inflation risks** rather than saying the risks were balanced, Brad’s time‑specific prediction did **not** come true.
predictions.grok_explanation:
The U.S. Federal Reserve did not publicly characterize its outlook as seeing a more balanced risk between economic growth and inflation by mid-summer 2022. Instead, official communications emphasized heightened inflation risks skewed to the upside, with growth risks skewed to the downside.

- **June 15, 2022 FOMC Statement** ([federalreserve.gov](https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/pressreleases/monetary20220615a.htm)): "The Committee is highly attentive to inflation risks."
- **Powell Press Conference Transcript, June 15** ([federalreserve.gov](https://www.federalreserve.gov/mediacenter/files/FOMCpresconf20220615.pdf)): Inflation risks "weighted to the upside"; no balanced risks mentioned; economy strong but inflation prioritized.
- **June 14-15 FOMC Minutes** ([federalreserve.gov](https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/fomcminutes20220615.htm)): "risks to the baseline projection for real activity were skewed to the downside and... risks to the inflation projection were skewed to the upside."
- **July 27, 2022 FOMC Statement** ([federalreserve.gov](https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/pressreleases/monetary20220727a.htm)): Reiterated "highly attentive to inflation risks."
- **July 26-27 FOMC Minutes** ([federalreserve.gov](https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/fomcminutes20220727.htm)): Growth risks "primarily... to the downside"; "balance of inflation risks remained skewed to the upside."

Balanced risk characterizations appeared later (e.g., May 2024 FOMC statement).
